finding.headline: Delaying Social Security past full retirement age raises the benefit until age 70.
details: Social Security retirement benefits increase for each month you delay starting them past full retirement age. The increase stops when you reach age 70.
Medicare generally starts when you turn 65. If you delay Medicare sign-up past that, you may face a monthly late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B coverage.
Your partner is age 62, so the household should compare benefit timing for both of you rather than assume one start date.

finding.headline: Plan for your money to last to age 98.
Working, you pay no tax on pay. In retirement, about 7% of withdrawals goes to tax.
details: Your plan shows a tax rate of 7% on money you take out in retirement, about $8,072 a year.
Most of your savings, about 68%, sits in pre-tax accounts like a 401(k). Draw on taxable savings first, then pre-tax accounts, and Roth accounts last.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Check the order with a tax professional before you draw money.

finding.headline: This household has no children, pets, or college costs to plan for.
details: Your basic yearly costs in retirement come to about $45,900, or $3,825 a month. Housing is $13,740, food $7,515, transport $12,138, and health $12,475.
Your mortgage ends in 2052, and your yearly costs drop by $4,800 after that. Before Medicare at age 65, health premiums are about $10,000 a year.
A nursing home stay could cost about $129,575 a year, for about 3 years. The plan does not include long-term care insurance.

finding.headline: Your spending goal lasts in 97 of 100 market scenarios, so the plan looks sound.
details: The plan kept is the plan of a similar household, which holds about 19% in stocks. The most you can spend each year and still be safe in 90 of 100 scenarios is $151,500, above your goal of $142,000. Your goal runs out in 3 of 100 scenarios.
Your median savings at retirement are $3,276,000 and at age 98 they are $1,441,000. In a weak market, savings at age 98 could fall as low as $355,000.
Markets are uncertain. These results are estimates, not promises, and a bad run of returns early in retirement could change the outcome.

finding.headline: You can count on $151,500 a year: $45,900 for basics and $105,600 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $45,900 a year.
Your goal is $142,000 a year, which is below the $151,500 that is safe, so the plan works.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
You already get Social Security (from 67): the plan uses the $27,600 a year you gave.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $18,400 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 98. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
